title: Random variables & distributions
blurb: Sample space, p(x), pdf vs probability, cdf

hook.title: One kilogram of sand
hook.text: Imagine you must spread exactly **1 kg of sand** over every outcome a random variable could take. For a die, you make six little piles; no pile can weigh more than 1 kg, and together they weigh exactly 1 kg. For something continuous, like tomorrow's temperature, you spread the sand as a smooth layer: the *height* of the layer at a point is the density, and what carries weight is the sand between two points.
hook.recall: Remember the sand: the total must be 1 kg. A discrete pile is a probability (≤ 1), but a squeezed, tall continuous layer can be higher than 1 because only the area counts.

explore.intro: Two ways to spread the sand. Switch tabs.
tasks: Discrete tab: change the raw weights. What happens to the bar labels? Can Σp(x) ever be anything but 1?
Continuous tab: shrink $\sigma$. Does the peak density go above 1? Does the shaded area ever exceed 1?
explore.takeaway: Discrete: each $p(x)\in[0,1]$ and they sum to 1. Continuous: $f(x)\ge 0$ and $\int f=1$; probabilities are *areas*, so $f(x)$ itself can exceed 1.

build.prompt: Turn raw pixel counts from a dataset into a valid distribution $p(x)$. Put the steps in order.
items: Count how many times each pixel value (0..255) occurs in the data
Divide every count by the total number of pixels counted
Check that each $p(x)$ lies between 0 and 1
build.explanation: This is exactly the empirical form on the slides: $P(x=x_i)=n_i/\sum n$. Dividing by the total guarantees the pile heights are in [0,1] and sum to 1.

questions.explanation: Every valid distribution sums to 1 over the sample space $\Omega$. That is the 1 kg of sand: you can move it between outcomes but never add or remove any.

questions.prompt: Which statement about probability distributions is FALSE?
options: For continuous $x$ the density $f(x)$ can never exceed 1
questions.explanation: A density is height of the sand layer, not an amount of sand. Squeeze the layer narrow and the height goes above 1 while the total area stays 1. Only the integral must equal 1.

questions.prompt: Three pixel values have probabilities $p(0)=0.2$ and $p(128)=0.5$. The only other value is 255. What is $p(255)$?
A student says: *“My narrow Gaussian has $f(0)=2.5$. That’s impossible, because probabilities can’t exceed 1.”* What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing, a valid pdf must have $f(x)\le1$
$f(0)$ is a density, not a probability. Only $\int f\,dx$ (areas) must be 1
The Gaussian must be wider so that $\sigma\ge1$
A pdf can be negative, so 2.5 is fine
questions.explanation: The student confused height with weight. $P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)dx$ is the probability; $f(0)$ alone is a density and can be large when the layer is narrow.

questions.prompt: If $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$ is the cdf, then $P(a\le X\le b)$ equals:
questions.explanation: The cdf is the sand to the left of $x$. The sand between $a$ and $b$ is the sand left of $b$ minus the sand left of $a$ (equivalently $\int_a^b f$).
